title: THE SHIELD WITH AN OPEN DOOR
deck: Ivara is dismantling the locks in Aster City's sky with her bare hands, and a meteor storm arrives in less than a day. Illuminara has one afternoon to learn what the locks once did to her.
shape: Six scenes across a day and a half: a sabotage interrupted, the first locked street, the prefect's ledger, a night at the bench where the saboteur finds the flaw in the design, a live test that fails once on purpose and is then rerun, and a storm held open.

scenes.title: The Lock, Not the Sky
paragraphs: *Terrace Nine relay hall, Aster City · the afternoon before the storm, 14:10*

Aster City lived under a lattice that cut the sky into twelve cells, with partitions between them that could be sealed. Illuminara reached Terrace Nine as the thirty-second closure relay came apart: a dry whine, like a wet finger on glass, and then a silence in the shape of a missing thing.

A woman stood with her bare palm flat against the cabinet door, light running off her fingers and down the metal. Two technicians pressed against the far wall with their hands raised. Nobody had threatened them. They had been told what she could do.

**Ivara** 
Stay where you are. I'm nearly done with this one.

**Illuminara** 
Thirty-two of forty-nine days, Ivara. Not one emitter among them.

**Ivara** 
The prefect says I'm tearing down the sky.

**Illuminara** 
The damage map says something narrower. Every cabinet you've opened was wound to push inward and seal a cell. You walked past three outward coils to reach this one.

**Ivara** 
Then you've read it. Do what you came to do.

**Illuminara** 
I came to ask why, because the council stopped listening after your first sentence.

The light on Ivara's fingers flared. A loose arc leapt from the broken cabinet toward the nearer technician, a boy of nineteen who had forgotten to breathe. Illuminara was between them before it finished curving. She took it through her shoulder and ran it down into the floor along a path she chose. It hurt. She did not remark on it.

**Ivara** 
I didn't aim that.

**Illuminara** 
I know. You're furious and your hands are very good. Both are true tonight.

**Ivara** 
Thirty-one years ago the sky over Low Marrow had a door on it, and the door was shut from outside. Four thousand people, six streets, eleven days, for our own protection. For three days we knocked. I was eight.

**Illuminara** 
Then I understand what you're breaking. Not yet what it costs. These relays do two jobs: they seal a cell, and they trade load between neighbours. You took the second out with the first. The front arrives in twenty-three hours, and it will find the thinnest cell and lean there.

**Ivara** 
Then they'll build another lock.

**Illuminara** 
Yes, unless someone builds a shield that can't be turned into one. Has anyone asked the people who were inside to design it?

**Ivara** 
They'd have to ask the man who kept the ledger.

**Illuminara** 
Prefect Vael.

**Ivara** 
He signed the closure. He still keeps the file.

**Illuminara** 
Then I'll ask him. First, show me the street.
Ivara took her hand from the cabinet. It was the first time in nine days she had lowered it by choice, and the technicians did not move, as though the room might change its mind.

scenes.title: The First Locked Street
paragraphs: *Low Marrow, Ward Nine, the water-plant gate · 16:20*

The doors in Ward Nine had handles on the outside only. Thirty-one years of paint had not hidden their inner faces: low on each one, scored into the wood at the height of a child's reach, groups of five scratches crossed by a sixth.
Illuminara laid her palm over one tally. She had once held a corridor open between two habitats for six hours and thought it the hardest door she would ever keep. She was less sure now.
A woman in water-plant overalls watched from the gate with her arms folded. Her tag read TEO MARSH.

**Teo** 
That one's mine. Eleven days of it. Please don't count.

**Illuminara** 
I wasn't going to. I was going to ask what you would need in order to trust a sky again.

**Teo** 
Not a speech. The prefect has made speeches. Ask your friend what her tour did to Sixth Terrace. My sister's dialysis ward is in that cell, and it ran on a lopsided field all night.

**Ivara** 
I know where it is.

**Teo** 
Then you know what it cost, and you're going to mend it with those hands on my crew's clock. After that you can tell me what you think of locks.
Ivara said nothing, and did not look away.

**Teo** 
Here's the test I would sign. Nine thousand of us in the street, lights off, a door at every partition, the prefect's own people at the console trying their hardest to close one. If a single door closes, it's a prison with better manners.

**Ivara** 
He'll cheat.

**Teo** 
Then I'll watch him cheat. That's what a test is.

**Illuminara** 
Twelve doors, one per boundary, each a baffled passage: two gates a body-length apart. The inner yields to a hand and springs shut behind it; the outer holds until the inner is closed. Springs and pins, not code. A lever on both faces, and half the keys held by people from this ward.

**Teo** 
The prefect holds the other half, and he'll say no first.

scenes.title: What the Prefect Kept
paragraphs: *Council Hall, the north chamber · 19:40*
Prefect Oren Vael had put the ledger on the table before she asked, which was the first unprompted honest act of his tenure, and he knew it.

**Vael** 
The closure order is on page four. I signed it as deputy. I was twenty-six. The hospital said the fever spread by contact, and it did not. I could not believe I was wrong, because then I had locked four thousand people in on a guess.

**Illuminara** 
You were wrong. And they are standing in the corridor outside this chamber.

**Vael** 
I know who is outside. Now hear the other half, because nobody will say it to you kindly. Seals save lives. Cinder Row, twenty years ago: we sealed eleven minutes late and lost two thousand to smoke. Your twelve doors are twelve holes, and holes cost a quarter of the field's efficiency whether anyone walks through them or not. What do I tell the next district when it burns and I could not contain it?

**Illuminara** 
That you chose which risk to share, and with whom. These aren't holes. They're the baffles I described to Teo: one gate always shut against smoke, both yielding to a hand. Slower than your seal, safer than your lock. I can't promise the dead are fewer in every fire. I can promise the people standing in the cell will make that call, not the one at a console.

**Vael** 
You are asking me to give them a veto over my own emergency powers.

**Illuminara** 
I'm asking you to put your hand on the lever beside theirs. Tomorrow you sit at the console as the adversary. If you close a door, the design fails and I will say so in this hall myself.

**Vael** 
And if it passes?

**Illuminara** 
Then there's an inquiry, and the ledger is the first exhibit.
Vael was silent long enough for the clock above the dais to change minutes. Then he slid the ledger across the table with two fingers, as one pushes a plate toward a guest.

**Vael** 
Thirty-one years. I wanted someone to ask me to do that. I did not expect it to be you.

scenes.title: Reversed Coil
paragraphs: *Terrace Nine workshop · night, 03:15*

Ivara sat at a bench among Teo's crew, rewinding a closure coil into a balance coil, handling the reversed windings like a sleeping animal. The tag read SIXTH TERRACE; Teo had asked for that relay first, and had not asked twice.

**Ivara** 
Why did you take that arc? You could have let it hit the boy and held me to it.

**Illuminara** 
There wasn't time to be good. It was going to hit a boy.

**Ivara** 
That's a stupid answer.

**Illuminara** 
It's the true one. The kind answer takes an hour.

Ivara laughed, once, startled, and then looked at her own hands as though they had done it without permission. Illuminara had been waiting for that sound all day, and was glad in a plain, undignified way, and did not hide it.

A mock exit stood at the end of the bench: two gates on a frame, built from the afternoon's drawings. Ivara put down the coil, picked up a pry bar, and approached it as one approaches an enemy one respects.

**Illuminara** 
Break it.

**Ivara** 
You want the person who wrecked thirty-two relays to attack your door.

**Illuminara** 
I want the person who knows exactly where doors fail.

She worked at it for forty minutes. At the thirty-first the bar went in behind the inner gate and caught the return cam, and the outer gate, which shared that cam, swung to as well. Both gates sat shut under one pair of hands.

**Ivara** 
There. One bar, one person, both gates held. It's a seal with a door painted on it.

**Teo** 
How long?

**Ivara** 
Thirty-one minutes. Faster if I weren't ashamed.

**Illuminara** 
What stops it?

**Ivara** 
Two cams, not one. And a shear pin in each gate's spring housing, set to break under the weight of a hand. A lock needs a key. A pin that breaks needs nobody. It's the one part of this I'd stake my name on, and my name isn't worth much this week.

**Teo** 
Draw it.

She drew it on the back of the Sixth Terrace work order. The pin was cheap, brass, and half the length of a finger, and Teo had them stamp I.K. on the inside of each housing, where nobody would look, so that in thirty years someone could find whom to ask. By morning the crew had cut cams and pins for four exits. Exit Seven was not among them. Teo wanted the old gate tested once, as it stood.

scenes.title: Nine Thousand Volunteers
paragraphs: *Terrace Seven plaza, Aster City · the morning of the storm, 06:10*

Nine thousand volunteers filled the plaza and the streets below it, most in dressing gowns and work boots, every light on every terrace out. At the hall console Prefect Vael had been told, in front of everyone, to close any door he could by any means he liked. He had nodded once.
At minute four the crowd pushed toward Exit Seven, and the old partition shut with a thud felt through every boot.

**Teo** 
Vael. Was that you?

**Vael** 
My hands are flat on the desk. Check the camera.

**Illuminara** 
It isn't him. It's the dispatch rule. Any crowd denser than six to a square metre counts as a fault, and the nearest partition seals to protect flow. Someone wrote it to be kind to the trams.
Teo's crew had the lever across in forty seconds. A woman with a toddler on her hip stood pinned against the gate, and no one was hurt, and everyone had seen it.

**Teo** 
Test passed. The door failed it, so the test did its job. Write that down.

**Illuminara** 
The dispatch rule goes from latch to lamp. It tells the crews where the crowd is thick and does nothing else.

**Vael** 
Metering will be rougher. People will be hurt at the doors.

**Illuminara** 
Fewer than behind them. We'll count together, you and Teo, and publish the count.

The crew fitted Exit Seven between eight and ten, with Ivara at the lathe. At ten o'clock they ran the same plaza again, and the front rank, by luck or by Teo's malice, held the same woman and the same toddler.

The crowd leaned. At ten past six that lean had been a wall. Now the pin in the inner housing gave at the weight of her shoulder, the leaf swung in, and she and her child stepped into the gap. The leaf shut behind them. Only then did the outer one open.

**Vael** 
Thirty-eight kilograms at the pin. The old gate held at four hundred, or until a man at a console let go of it.
He said it flatly, to the board. For the next eleven minutes, while nine thousand people went through, he tried every trick he had, and nothing closed.
At Exit Twelve, Teo held out a brass key to Ivara.

**Teo** 
You've broken thirty-two of ours. Break one that's meant to break.

Ivara turned the key. The gates drew back. She put her palm to the latch and pushed with everything she had learned to unmake, and found a spring, a brass pin and nothing in the field to take hold of.

**Ivara** 
There's nothing here to break.

**Teo** 
That's the idea.

**Ivara** 
Then ask me again in three months. First day of the quarter, in the plaza, at a bench, in public, with my bar and your key beside it. I'll try to break it until I can't.
She said it to the gate, not to the council, and no one had asked her to.

scenes.title: The Door Stays Open
paragraphs: *Northern arc above Weir Terrace · the storm, 13:35*

By noon eight of the twelve exits had their new cams: Five through Twelve, the evacuation routes first. One to Four kept their old gates, pinned open with a crew on each and no seal to fall. At Exit Three a file of nine hundred had taken forty minutes and bruised a hundred and ten of them.

The retrofit left the northern arc dark for thirty-eight minutes while the rewound lattice charged, and Illuminara held it herself. While she held the sky she could do nothing else, so everything else had to belong to someone who could. The stones came down against her palms like rain on a very large window, and she thought, absurdly, of five scratches crossed by a sixth.
The city reached her through a radio at her ear.
A fragment slipped through the thinner cell and Weir Market caught fire. The old logic would have sealed the cell around the blaze and kept the smoke in with the people.

**Teo** 
Exit Five. Opening.

**Vael** 
I'm at the lever beside you, Marsh. Sealing is off.

At Exit Five a file of twelve stepped into the gap, the inner gate sprang shut behind them, and only then did the outer give way onto clean air. Twenty-two seconds a file. Vael had moved the smoke gauge onto his own board that morning, and he read it aloud over the radio, as a man says a number he has argued with.

**Vael** 
Four parts in a hundred reaching the next cell. A seal would have been none. An open door would have been thirty-one. Keep them coming.

Six thousand people walked out of the Weir cell in a line, and crews stood at every gate. The smoke travelled with them farther than Vael had wanted. Forty-one were treated for it, two shops burned to the frames, and no one was locked in.
When the lattice came back, Illuminara lowered her arms. Down on Terrace Nine, Ivara stood at Exit Twelve with Teo's brass key, and neither of them was speaking.

The council signed for the costs in daylight: a quarter of the field's efficiency gone for good, three terraces sheltering underground until the rewinding was done, four exits still to fit, an inquiry on Thursday in which Vael would testify first and Ivara would answer for thirty-two relays. Half the keys were in the hands of people from Low Marrow. Nobody pretended the forgiveness was owed.

**Teo** 
My sister's pumps ran at sixty percent for a night. She's home. I haven't decided what I think about that, and neither of you gets to decide it for me.

**Ivara** 
No.

**Vael** 
No.
The door at Exit Twelve stayed open all that night, and the people who walked through it did so for no reason at all, which was the whole of the proof.

critic_line: A shield built from the saboteur's own wound and tested by the man who signed the first lock, proven by a door that stays open for no reason at all.
